03 · Why design matters

You aren't designing screens.
You're designing someone's money.

A confusing screen here isn't just bad UX. It's someone's financial future on the line. Our users span all of India: someone opening their first account and someone trading daily use the same product, and both need to trust it. Carry that responsibility with care, and it becomes the most meaningful part of the job.

Our mission
Helping every Indian confidently Up their wealth.

Every design decision moves someone one step further along this path. That's the responsibility, and the privilege.

05 · Culture & how we work

How we think,
how we work.

A few things we believe about how design should operate here. Not poster values, actual working rules.

Decide, don't wait.

Sometimes the PRD won't hand you a clear answer. When there's no decision maker in the room, you can be one. Do your research first, and be ready to explain why you went the way you did. We call this the silver line of design.

Align early, surprise no one.

For anything new, get regular alignment with design stakeholders before product sees it. Most confusion and last-minute drama on projects comes from skipping this. Don't skip this.

Confidence, not stress.

We don't take stress, we take decisions and move ahead. Stay flexible when new information lands, but keep moving. A team stuck waiting for perfect clarity ships nothing.

Your buddy

Every new designer gets a buddy, assigned by HR when you join. Usually someone in your city and, where possible, your function: product design, DS, or communication design. We rotate this among the team, mostly PD1s and PD2s, so everyone gets a turn at it.

Your buddy is your first stop for the unwritten stuff: which channel, which file, who to ask, where lunch is. +

Lean on them through your first few weeks, and no question is too small. They'll point you to the right Slack channels, the current production files, who owns what, and the little rituals that aren't written down anywhere.

08 · Design process

Every project follows the same shape.

Tap a step to see what it means. You don't need to memorise this, your buddy will walk you through it live.

01
Scoping & sizing+

Understand the problem and agree how big it is before you draw anything. This is where you decide what's in and out.

02
Wireframes+

Low-fidelity structure and flow. Explore directions fast. This is a great place to use Claude + Odin.

03
Internal reviewNon-negotiable+

Design critiques design. This always comes before product review, no exceptions.

04
Product review+

Align with product on the solution. Come with more than one idea and the reasoning behind your choice.

05
DS audit+

The design system team checks your file is built correctly on Arc, so it flows cleanly into code.

06
Feasibility checkIf complex+

On technically complex work, get a feasibility call with engineering done before handover.

07
Production file+

The clean, Arc-built file engineering will actually work from. It follows the production standards in the process guide.

08
Handover → Engineering+

Handover Pending means design is done. Once a track hits Engineering Backlog, your job on it is done.

09
Pixel PerfectionNon-negotiable+

Once it lands on a real test build, sit with your engineers, review the design live, and do the final round of pixel perfection so it ships exactly as intended.

20th

Every track must reach Handover Pending.

30th

All handovers completed. Engineering won't pick up new tracks after this.

Confidence

Each track carries a High / Medium / Low ship rating. Low-confidence tracks tend to slip, so weight them less.

09 · Your first 90 days

Three cycles. Consider it a quest.

We run on monthly cycles, so think of your ramp as three of them. The pace flexes by seniority, so agree the specifics with your manager in week one.

Cycle 1Learn the machine
Get your access sorted and meet the team.
Open an Upstox account, place a trade, start an SIP. You can't design for investors if you've never invested.
Sit in on internal reviews and one full handover.
Ship one small thing through the real pipeline.
Outcome

You understand how the machine works, and one small thing of yours has shipped.

Cycle 2Run a track
Own a well-scoped track end to end, into Handover Pending before the 20th.
Do your first DS audit with the design system team.
Start giving feedback in other designers' reviews, not just receiving it.
Outcome

You've carried a track through the full pipeline on your own timeline.

Cycle 3Operate like a pro
Own a track of real scope, through handover, without hand-holding.
Spot one thing about our process or the DS that's broken or slow, and propose a fix.
Sit with your manager: what worked in your ramp, what didn't, what this guide got wrong.
Outcome

You operate like you've been here a year, and you've made the place a little better.

10 · Interesting stories

Things you'd otherwise pick up over chai.

A short walk through where we came from. Tap a year to open it.

2010
It began as RKSV Securities.+

The name came from the founders' initials. Opening an account meant a 30-page form, printed and couriered to the office. A lot of the journey from there is a design story.

2016
The Upstox app arrived.+

It launched with the industry's first paperless account opening, and the 30-page form eventually came all the way down to zero.

2020
10 lakh customers.+

Then 1 crore by 2022, which is 10x in under two years. Nearly 70% were first-time investors, and more than 85% came from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities. That's who you're designing for.

2021
Unicorn.+

Upstox entered the unicorn club after a Tiger Global-led round. Ratan Tata was an early investor.

Today
Designing for millions.+

The design team was 5 people in 2017, around 21 by 2024, roughly 30 today across two cities. We once did research sitting in traders' homes, part of a 14-month redesign with a global agency.

The lesson

We ran Pro and Invest as two modes for years. That was twice the work, and users kept asking for the same features in both. So we're unifying into one app. The right architecture is the one you can actually sustain.

11 · Design IP & confidentiality

The work we make stays with Upstox.

Anything you design here belongs to Upstox, and a few simple habits keep it safe. None of this is meant to feel scary, it’s the same at any design job. Ask before you take anything out, assume your activity is visible, and you’ll never have to think about it again.

Whose work is it?

Anything you design here is Upstox's, whether you're staff, consultant, or vendor. Shipped or not, it's ours.

What needs the most care

Live work, ideas we never shipped, and our design system. Even a rough idea shows how we think.

Being able to export isn't permission

An export, a screenshot, and a photo of your screen are the same. What makes it okay is permission, not the format.

Yes, activity is logged

Figma and company devices log activity. If something looks off, we check in first and only escalate if needed.

Spot a leak? Tell InfoSec

Spot something shared externally, yours or anyone's? Flag InfoSec right away. First stop for everyone.

Need to take something out? Ask first.

Portfolio or testing in another tool is fine. Tell your manager why and get a yes in writing before you export.

Leaving or wrapping up a contract

Don't build a personal “everything I made” folder on your way out. Unreleased work comes out first, checked with your manager.

Consultants and vendors

A signed IP agreement comes before Figma or repo access, never after. It covers your company too, not just you.

If you're asked to explain an export

It's about understanding, not blame. Expect a few quick questions: what, when, why, where it went, and who's seen it.
